With a capacity of 5.0 million tonnes per year (MTY), Maheshpur RLS is BCCL’s first First Mile Connectivity (FMC) project and enables mechanised and rapid loading of coal into railway rakes, supporting faster and more efficient coal evacuation. The first rake loaded through the facility was dispatched to NTPC Nabinagar, marking the commencement of coal evacuation through the facility.

The achievement follows a series of key milestones completed during 2026, including rail connectivity with the Main DC line, Non-Interlocking (NI) work, the diesel engine trial and approval of commercial notification by the Railway Authority.

The successful operationalisation of Maheshpur RLS reflects the coordinated efforts of BCCL, Indian Railways, State authorities, executing agencies and other stakeholders. Speaking on the occasion, CMD Shri Manoj Kumar Agarwal said that the project will give a further boost to BCCL's First Mile Connectivity initiatives and make coal evacuation more efficient.

Also present on the occasion were GM (Govindpur) Shri Satyakam Anand, GM (Barora) Shri K.K. Singh, GM (UG & Siding) Shri G.K. Mehta, GM (E&M) Shri R.R. Karan and Project Officer (Maheshpur Silo) Shri Dhiraj Kumar, along with other senior officials.

Coal Is Back in the Global Energy Mix

The Middle East conflict is creating an unexpected winner in the energy market: coal.

Disruptions to LNG shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have pushed gas prices higher, making coal-fired generation more competitive. The IEA now expects global coal demand to rise 1.2% to 8.94 billion tonnes in 2026, a record high.

The price response is already visible. Newcastle 6,000-kcal thermal coal reached $148.29 a tonne by mid-September, while South Korea's coal-fired power generation jumped 39.7% year-on-year in April.

Supply is tightening too. Indonesia, the world's largest thermal-coal exporter, has reportedly cut its 2026 production quota to 600 million tonnes, down 24% from the previous year.

For India, this matters because higher international coal prices can affect power-generation costs, imported coal economics and domestic coal demand.

The key Indian names to watch are Coal India, NTPC, NLC India and Singareni Collieries-linked ecosystem, while imported-coal exposure makes the picture more complicated for some power producers.

The Mercator Take

The energy transition doesn't always move in a straight line.

When gas becomes expensive and LNG supply is disrupted, countries with available coal capacity can quickly turn back to coal.

The immediate lesson is that energy security can temporarily override energy-transition economics.

If Hormuz disruptions persist, coal could remain an important second-order beneficiary of the energy shock.

Uncertainty carries with it vulnerability, its comforting to have certainty, it feels secure, safe, and you feel proficient for having it. 

Philosophy of science, epistimology, shows that uncertainty reigns, that you can't disprove alternate theories by piling on evidence, that all facts gathered are filtered through your sense data, reason, and access to information, that facts run into a wall of infinite regress, cyclical logic, or hear say. 

This causes uncertainty. 

This uncertainty is very strongly made clear in the world religions. 

Buddhism and hinduism calls it, among other things, netti netti (not this, not this)

In Buddhism its also called 

Anabhilāpya (ineffable / unutterable)

Apanihita (aimless / ungraspable).

Taoism calls it Wuming (nameless) and Xuan (mystery)

In Christianity its called Mysterion

In Hinduism its called Anirvacanīya (अनिर्वचनीय): The formal technical term in Advaita Vedanta for that which is indescribable, indefinable, or indeterminate.

Avyakta (अव्यक्त): "Unmanifest," "unexpressed," or "indistinct"

Apanihita / Acintya (अचिन्त्य): "Inconceivable" or "beyond the grasp of the rational mind."

In Zen, this suspended uncertainty is often called Fushin (unknowing mind / "don't-know mind")

In zen its also explained using the analogy of "the finger pointing at the moon"

Words are like the finger, the finger is not the moon, the finger points your attention to the moon and helps you realize and behold the moon. 

Words are not the concepts, the words point your attention to the concepts and helps you realize and behold the concepts. 

Realizing and beholding the concept, beyond words, is called "satori". 

Kant pointed out it applied to science and reason and called it Fideism

Kant argued that, while we can't know something, we can't have knowledge of the thing unto it self, we can have a regulative idea, we can continuously derive benefit from pursuing what is ultimately an impossible goal to realize. 

This concept is similar to the Christian concept of theosis and epektasis, an infinite process of becoming more like god and understanding gods inconceivable nature, something that is ultimately impossible to achieve.

Odisha’s Aluminium Boom Needs a Full Accounting

A proposed ₹1.8 lakh crore aluminium ecosystem, ₹1 lakh crore already invested, ₹9,000 crore reportedly contributed annually to Odisha’s exchequer, and a claimed 3% contribution to the state’s GDP sound impressive—but investment headlines are not the same as public benefit. What is the independently audited figure after subtracting subsidies, tax concessions, land, water, electricity, public infrastructure, environmental damage, and rehabilitation costs?

If Vedanta’s Odisha operations account for 40–45% of India’s aluminium production, why is the public not being shown complete data on local employment, wages, contract labour, displacement, health impacts, water use, emissions, ash and red-mud management, and compliance violations? If the company is a major contributor to Odisha’s economy, will it publish plant-wise taxes, royalties, energy consumption, pollution readings, and community spending in a verifiable format?

The contradiction is simple: industrial expansion may generate revenue and jobs, but the same expansion can impose costs on communities and ecosystems. Who receives the profits, and who bears the pollution, land, water, and health risks? Will the government release an independent cost–benefit assessment before calling Odisha the “aluminium capital” of India?

Development should not mean that corporate scale is celebrated while citizens are asked to remain silent about public costs. Publish the numbers, disclose the risks, enforce the law, and let Odisha’s people decide whether this is inclusive development—or merely an expanding corporate footprint.
